So I thought I'd share this little "trick" I used in school. If you want to make a pattern ,or have a pattern in say scale 1:4 and want to make it the actual size you need, you just use math!

Say I have a full size pattern of a skirt that I want to make in a smaller scale in order to change the pattern, and save paper/space, I would go about it like this.

Example: Skirt measurements waist 70 cm- hip 80 cm- butt 85 cm- length 100 cm to make it a scale 1:4 all you have to do is divide the measurements with 4.

This will leave you with waist 17.5 cm - hip 20 cm- butt 21.25 cm- length 25 cm then you just draw out your pattern with those measurements and do any changes you want

Say I wanted to add 20 cm to the skirts length I would add 5 cm on the 1:4 scale pattern. You can make any changes you want to a pattern no matter how complicated or easy they might be. Its a good way if you wanna try different designs, if you are unsure what you want or just for practice.

When you are done with your pattern you simply take the measurements x 4 and draw out your full size pattern.

Sounds like an open and shut case of Tortious Interference

A lot of people put stock in tortious interference when these things come up but its misguided for two reasons:

  1. The conduct which induces the party to the breach must, of itself, be tortious. There is nothing tortious about bringing factual matters to the attention of the contracting party (in this case, the employer). Making false representations or threats would meet the test, but informing the employer and even making demands would not.

  2. There is nothing unlawful about inducing a party to terminate a contract lawfully, they have to be inducing a breach of the contract. It's worth noting that breaching employment law statutes as regards unfair dismissal, wrongful termination etc is not the same as breaching a contract. It is possible to unfairly dismiss/wrongfully terminate an employee without having breached the employment contract.

Japanese courts agree:

Asahikawa District Court on Dec. 27, 1989, ruled against a company (Hankiko Setsubi) that fired a female employee but not a male one after discovering the two were committing adultery.

Management reasoned that even if it does not interfere with work, “adultery adversely affects the company’s moral order, hurts coworkers’ motivation, and makes the president lose face.” While acknowledging that the woman’s actions were illegal and immoral, the court said that only specific damage to the running of the company constitutes hurting the workers’ moral order or motivation, a condition not met in this case.

Thus judicial precedent prohibits disciplinary action for problematic personal behavior that has no connection with work duties. Meanwhile, only if such personal actions severely damage a company’s overall reputation can they be considered to have seriously damaged the company’s moral order.
